title: Annotated Bibliography
text:
Citations

Addo, F. R., Sassler, S., & Williams, K. (2016). Reexamining the Association of Maternal Age and Marital Status at First Birth With Youth Educational Attainment. Journal of Marriage and Family, 78(5), 1252–1268. https://doi.org/10.1111/jomf.12360

Addo, Sassler, and Williams (2016) use data from the Children and Young Adult sample of the 1979 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth to examine how maternal age and marital status at birth influence children’s chances of completing high school. The study finds that children of older teen mothers are no more likely to graduate than those of younger teen mothers. However, children born to young adult mothers (ages 20–24) have higher odds of finishing high school than those born to teen mothers, though they remain at a disadvantage compared to children whose mothers were 25 or older at birth. The authors also find that being born to an unmarried mother lowers the likelihood of high school completion, regardless of race or ethnicity. Overall, this study highlights the persistent educational disadvantages linked to early and nonmarital childbearing and underscores the importance of maternal age and family structure in shaping children’s educational outcomes.

Akanbi, Moses A., et al. “Influence of Socio-Economic Factors on Prevalence of Teenage Pregnancy in Nigeria.” African Journal of Reproductive Health, vol. 25, no. 5s, 2021, pp. 138–46, https://doi.org/10.29063/ajrh2021/v25i5s.13.

Akanbi argues that religious affiliation, socio-economic status, child marriage, and education level play a large role in early pregnancy rates in Nigeria citing hard evidence of these phenomena. The evidence that is presented is from a study regarding teenage pregnancy in Nigeria for women before the age of 20 years old. The correlations are clear that approximately a fifth of girls in ages 15-19 experienced teenage pregnancy in Nigeria. Akanbi also notes how girls from more rural areas and girls in Muslim families experience more teenage pregnancy. This resource is important as it cites critical statistics on how early pregnancy is induced by factors like location, religion, region, education, marital status, and family planning facilities. This resource specifically helps us target our thesis by affirming how lower educational levels leads to less knowledge on reproductive health care and therefore risks of pregnancy. It also reaffirms some of our side theses on economic status and religious influences on birth rates.

Azzopardi, Peter S., et al. “Progress in Adolescent Health and Wellbeing: Tracking 12 Headline Indicators for 195 Countries and Territories, 1990–2016.” The Lancet (British Edition), vol. 393, no. 10176, 2019, pp. 1101–18 https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)32427-9.

Azzopardi argues that while adolescent health has improved in some respects from 1990-2016, immense and substantial inequalities persist globally. The authors use data from 195 countries, measuring twelve key health indicators like fertility rates, education levels, nutrition, substance use, etc. This source is important because it provides a large-scale, data-driven overview of how adolescent health differs across regions and genders. It connects to the overall vision for our paper by showing that gender inequality, such as higher rates of child marriage, limited education, and poor reproductive health access, continues to negatively affect female health in developing countries. The authors show that diseases linked to poverty, like infections and malnutrition, have gone down, but because of population growth in poorer countries, more teens are still living in tough health conditions. Overall, the study says that schools, health systems, and laws have not kept up with the changes teens are facing, and that gender inequality continues to be a major reason why females in developing countries often have worse health outcomes than males.

Hagues, R. J., Bae, D., & Wickrama, K. K. A. S. (2017). Mediational Pathways Connecting Secondary Education and Age at Marriage to Maternal Mortality: A Comparison between Developing and Developed Countries. Women & Health, 57(2), 189–207. https://doi.org/10.1080/03630242.2016.1159266

Hagues, Bae, Wickrama argue that secondary education and the age at which women marry are crucial in reducing maternal mortality, but that these factors operate through ‘mediational pathways,’ or indirectly. Greater attainment of education and a later marriage age are associated with reduced maternal mortality. The study uses data from the national statistical databases of both developed and developing countries. This study is crucial in that it unlocks how education and marrying at a later age for women can prevent high rates of maternal mortality - leading to policy implications that could prevent unnecessary death during childbirth and beyond. The findings of this study provide evidence that through education, maternal mortality is somewhat avoidable. Because education attainment and marriage age is very gender-biased in both developing and developed countries, it is crucial to explore the imbalance between these factors.

Leybourne, G. G., & White, K. (1940). Education and the birth-rate, a social dilemma / by Grace G. Leybourne and Kenneth White, with a foreword by A.M. Carr Saunders, and an introd. by R.H. Tawney. J. Cape.

In this book, Leybourne and White explore the relationship between educational attainment, social class, and declining birth rates in early 20th-century Britain. The authors argue that rising educational opportunities, especially for women, contributed to changes in family planning, delayed marriage, and smaller family sizes, posing what they describe as a “social dilemma” for national population growth. The book displays demographic patterns within broader debates about social progress, gender roles, and economic stability. Although dated in its empirical methods and social assumptions, the book remains significant as an early attempt to link education and fertility within a sociological framework and provides valuable historical insight into early twentieth-century population issues.

McGillivray, Mark, et al., editors. Health Inequality and Development. Palgrave Macmillan UK, 2011. DOI.org (Crossref), https://doi.org/10.1057/9780230304673.

In this book, McGillivary argues that inequalities in developing countries, in particular, are intertwined with social, policy, and economic factors that can be found in health outcomes that demonstrate patterns of gendered disadvantage and exclusion in education. In terms of resources, it utilizes a variety of empirical chapters that feature micro and macro level data analysis. These analyses include case studies regarding child nutrition and female labor market participation. This resource links health inequalities to big societal issues such as lack of job opportunities and education. This source helps explain that in order to solve some of these issues, more action than simple medical care will need to be implemented. This book relates women’s education to societal inequality and reproductive and healthcare injustice.

Okonofua, Friday. « Economic Development and Reproductive Health in Africa / Développement économique et santé reproductive en Afrique ». African journal of reproductive health, vol. 1, no 2, 1997, p. 6‑9. https://search.library.ucla.edu/permalink/01UCS_LAL/192ecse/cdi_unpaywall_primary_10_2307_3583371

Okonofua presents in their piece that reproductive health in sub-Saharan African countries is generally inferior to other nations including the higher rate of sexually transmitted diseases, maternal mortality, infertility, and access to safe reproductive health services. Okonofua argues that this is due to the substandard socio-economic status and education levels of women in sub-Saharan Africa. The resource the author uses largely comes from the World Health Organization. This resource is so important because it highlights how poverty is one of the key contributing factors to reproductive health in these regions contributing to a lack of knowledge through education and lack of resources. This resource supports our thesis as this research is even showing that these conditions may even be worsening in several regions, with maternal mortality rates increasing in Nigeria.

Okui, T. (2023). Analysis of an Association between Preterm Birth and Parental Educational Level in Japan Using National Data. Children, 10(2), 342-. https://doi.org/10.3390/children10020342

Through this study, Okui displays how lower parental education level is linked to a higher rate of preterm birth risk. This study was conducted using data from national linked data sets of Japan, including census data and statistics from the national department of education. The findings in this study are important because they emphasize that a higher level of education can help to prevent the health risks of preterm births, both to the infant and to the parent. It provides empirical evidence that a higher level of education in both parents leads to safer births, potentially leading to the understanding that gender imbalance in education can lead to medical issues, especially in pregnant women.

Pezzulo, Carla, et al. “Geographical Distribution of Fertility Rates in 70 Low-Income, Lower-Middle-Income, and Upper-Middle-Income Countries, 2010–16: A Subnational Analysis of Cross-Sectional Surveys.” The Lancet Global Health, vol. 9, no. 6, 2021, pp. e802–12, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(21)00082-6.

Pezzulo argues through their research that in more rural and lower income areas, there are often high-fertility clusters. The research also demonstrates how rates of women with secondary education are higher in low-feritility clusters and areas with low contraceptive use are correlated with high-fertility clusters. This research is coming from clustering analysis of cross-sectional surveys across 70 countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the data was from demographic and health surveys, UNICEF, and multiple indicator cluster Surveys. This resource is critical as it identifies areas of low-fertility clusters and associated variable correlations in those regions, helping us pinpoint the factors influencing fertility rates in specific regions. In terms of our thesis, this specifically supports our hypothesis that region specific factors influence fertility rate and targeting variables like education level and access to reproductive resources lower fertility rates and can be targeted to specific high-fertility cluster regions.

Ran, Na. “Study of Impacts of Education, Open-Access Medical Publishing, and Internet on Women’s Health in China.” Health Care for Women International, vol. 44, no. 9, 2023, pp. 1273–89, https://doi.org/10.1080/07399332.2022.2096888.

Na Ran articulates that higher female education, greater internet access, and mobile phone usage, and wider availability of open-access medical research are all significantly associated with lower mortality rates among women and girls in China. The author utilizes quantitative analyses of national data on women’s mortality alongside indicators such as female school enrollment, mobile subscriptions, internet access, and counts of open-access medical articles, revealing strong negative correlations. This source is important because it shows how knowledge and information-based tools such as education, digital access, and scholarly publishing play a role in improving women’s health outcomes beyond just medical interventions. Regarding our topic on gendered health in developing countries, it provides evidence that access to education and digital/information resources can reduce gendered health disparities by empowering women with knowledge and connectivity that will complement and deepen our focus on gendered social determinants of health.

Rizvi, Javed H., and Nadeem F. Zuberi. “Women’s Health in Developing Countries.” Best Practice & Research Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology, vol. 20, no. 6, Dec. 2006, pp. 907–22. DOI.org (Crossref), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bpobgyn.2006.06.005.

Rizvi and Zuberi (2006) argue that women in developing countries face a large obstacle with gynaecological and reproductive health and that any improvement that is intended to be made in the field of women’s health requires community involvement, a variety of reforms, and proper resource allocation. The resource utilizes pre-existing synthesized sources from the Reproductive Health Library and the Cochrane Library. Additionally, some data and information can be categorized as clinical and regional epidemiological data. These resources were compiled to create a variety of data about the epidemiology of abortion, sexual health issues, and many other gynaecological problems experienced by women in developing countries. The importance of this resource lies in the open view it brings to women’s health in low-resource environments. It highlights the gaps in policy and knowledge that are present in some developing countries. This article provides context in relation to female education and reproductive health issues in developing countries by demonstrating how inadequate health services and gaps in policy weaken female reproductive health. This in turn affects educational and economic opportunities.

Saliba, Matilda, and Huda Zurayk. “Expanding Concern for Women’s Health in Developing Countries.” Women’s Health Issues, vol. 20, no. 3, May 2010, pp. 171–77. DOI.org (Crossref), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.whi.2010.01.001.

Saliba and Zurayk argue that women’s health in developing countries, particularly in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR), should be expanded beyond the constraints of reproductive health and reproductive ages, in order to include long-term conditions and health at different stages of age. They use epidemiological and public health data that details the implications and burdens of major non-communicable diseases among women in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. This journal article expands the scope of “women’s health” in developing countries. It highlights that focusing on only reproduction significantly misrepresents significant diseases and other non-maternal burdens. Although my thesis gears toward female education, fertility, and access to healthcare, this resource helps by broadening the scope. It highlights that women’s health outcomes, thus the value of their education and health access, extends beyond the regulated scope of fertility. It supports the argument that improving women’s education and healthcare access has implications not just for reproductive health, but for overall lifelong health.

Singh, Harpreet, and Rana Amanat Singh. “Gender and Inequality in Access to Healthcare Facilities in India: Evidence from NSSO’s 75th Round on Health.” Millennial Asia, 2023, https://doi.org/10.1177/09763996231195663.

In this article, Harpreet Singh and Rana Amanat Singh analyze gender inequalities in access to healthcare in India applying data from the National Sample Survey Office’s 75th Round on Health (2017–2018). The authors collaborated to have a Gender Parity Index (GPI) to measure the difference of both men and women’s difference in getting access to healthcare support. The research found that on an average, women are more likely to be facing barriers getting medical aid. Especially for women living in rural areas who are facing a double burden where there was a lack of resources and more relied on public or underdeveloped service. In comparison, males are more likely to get healthcare benefits and high-quality service such as private hospitals. The research argues that there’s a structural gender inequality, economical struggles and also a control under the patriarchal norms. The article concluded that there should be a policy constructed that focused on both accessibility and that are sensitive to gender norms. The article can be seen as valuable evidence that there’s a coexisting relationship between gender inequality, geographical locations and socioeconomic positions that are together impacting the national healthcare system of India.

Stange, K. (2011). A Longitudinal Analysis of the Relationship Between Fertility Timing and Schooling. Demography, 48(3), 931–956. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13524-011-0050-3

Stange (2011) conducts a longitudinal study examining how the timing of fertility influences women’s postsecondary educational attainment, with particular attention to dynamic selection processes. These processes capture how women’s educational and fertility decisions evolve together over time, reflecting not only fixed characteristics such as background or ability but also time-varying factors that lead some women to diverge from educational paths even before pregnancy occurs. Using a matching approach based on predicted birth hazard rates, Stange compares eventual mothers with non-mothers who share similar pre-pregnancy characteristics. The study finds that both groups initially enter college at similar rates, but their educational trajectories begin to differ before childbirth, suggesting that pre-pregnancy factors drive much of the observed educational gap. Stange concludes that conventional controls and fixed-effects models fail to account for this dynamic selection bias, highlighting the need for models that jointly consider fertility and educational decision-making. This research provides a nuanced understanding of how the timing and sequencing of life events shape women’s educational outcomes.

Tamir, Tadesse Tarik. “Neonatal Mortality Rate and Determinants among Births of Mothers at Extreme Ages of Reproductive Life in Low and Middle Income Countries.” Scientific Reports, vol. 14, no. 1, 12596, 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-61867-w.

This article argues that neonates born to mothers at the extreme ends of reproductive age, adolescents, and older mothers in low and middle-income countries face higher mortality risks compared to those born to mothers in the typical reproductive age range. The authors use secondary analysis of demographic and health survey data from 43 low and middle-income countries, including a total sample of 151,685 live births, and employ a multilevel mixed-effects model to identify specific determinants of neonatal mortality such as maternal education, home delivery, multiple births, country-level fertility, etc. This source is important because it highlights how maternal age as a social and biological factor intersects with other vulnerabilities, such as low education or home birth, to affect newborn survival in developing settings. This will support our project on gendered health in developing countries as it shows how maternal age, which often correlates with gendered norms such as early childbearing or older motherhood, can contribute to gender specific risks for newborns, thereby reinforcing the argument that gendered social factors shape health outcomes in low-income contexts.

World Health Organization. “Maternal Health.” WHO, 23 Sept. 2019, www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/maternal-health.


Yan, J., Wang, L., Yang, Y., Zhang, Y., Zhang, H., He, Y., Peng, Z., Wang, Y., Wang, Q., Shen, H., Zhang, Y., Yan, D., Ma, X., & Yang, H. (2020). The trend of caesarean birth rate changes in China after ‘universal two-child policy’ era: a population-based study in 2013–2018. BMC Medicine, 18(1), Article 249. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-020-01714-7

This study indicates that in China, the implementation of the two-child policy first led to a decline in caesarean birth rates, and then increased between two and three years after the policy was introduced. This study is based off of a population-based data set from the National Free Pre-Pregnancy Check-Ups Project, which included data from 31 provinces of mainland China from 2013-2018. Through this study, we can understand more about how large-scale policy changes can influence obstetric outcomes and demographic outcomes. This study highlights the gender-imbalanced variable of maternal health with respect to access and risk in health system practices. Because the C-section rate has implications for maternal and newborn health, it is crucial to investigate how these policy changes can affect men and women alike.

Zeng, Junxia, et al. “Gender Inequality in Education in China: A Meta-Regression Analysis.” Contemporary Economic Policy, vol. 32, no. 2, 2014, pp. 474–91, https://doi.org/10.1111/coep.12006.

Junxia Zeng and her team assessed the level of gender inequality in education and its trend in the late 20th century of China, by using metadata analysis. By examining many studies and researches, the author quantified the gender factors influencing educational success and outcomes. That there’s a difference in education outcomes and success rates in different areas, levels and times in China. The data have shown that although the level of education disparity is getting less, it still exists especially in rural areas and families with low incomes. The research pointed out that the gender inequality of China is largely due to poor socioeconomic positions, lack of implementation of policies and that Chinese society has a favor of sacrificing women’s education rights to their male relatives first. The conclusion stated that there should be an ongoing focus on ensuring the rights of education for women, especially in rural areas and underdeveloped provinces. This article provided a powerful example to how economic and education policies reforms can better shape gender equality in China.

title: Data Critique
text:
World Bank Gender Data Portal Logo



Dataset & Variables
We originally chose this dataset because it contained many variables that aligned with our research interests, spanning education, health, economic conditions, and gender equality. However, once we downloaded the full Gender Data Portal dataset and began preparing it for analysis, we encountered extensive missing values across many of the indicators we hoped to use. This forced us to work with subsets of the data rather than the complete set of variables we had planned to analyze. As a result, our final dataset represents only the indicators with sufficient coverage across countries and years, which inevitably leaves out important metrics and creates silences within our analysis. In other words, our findings reflect the structure of the available data—not necessarily the full complexity of global gender inequality.
The original sources for the Gender Data Portal include national governments and major international organizations that produce official gender-disaggregated statistics. These sources range from national statistical offices, ministries of labor, health, and education to global agencies such as UNDP, UNICEF, UNESCO, UN Women, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The World Bank compiles, standardizes, and harmonizes these national submissions so that cross-country comparisons become possible.
The World Bank Group funded the creation and maintenance of the Gender Data Portal, primarily through its Gender Group and the Development Economics Data Group. The Portal is updated four times per year and supported by additional contributions from multi-donor trust funds such as the Umbrella Facility for Gender Equality and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.
The dataset from 2000–2023 captures a wide range of interconnected dimensions of gender inequality, including:

Human Capital & Health: Indicators related to population health, healthcare access, and overall human capital development. These variables reflect overall human capital through the female-specific human capital index
Women’s Autonomy and Reproductive Health: These variables measure women’s empowerment in personal and reproductive decision-making and assess the degree of autonomy, reproductive rights, and access to reproductive health services among women.
Economic Indicators: These variables focus on the broader economic environment, income distribution, and the inclusiveness of economic growth.
Population & Demographic: The demographic variables provide basic structural information about a country’s population, including total population size and the proportion of females.
Education: Education indicators reflect gender parity and access to schooling across different levels. These variables provide insights into gender equality in educational attainment and investment in human capital formation.
Labor Force & Education Level: Labor force indicators describe the distribution of educational attainment among working-age populations, disaggregated by gender.
Gender Equality & Institutional Factors: These variables include institutional-level measures of gender equality

Variables such as the Human Capital Index (HCI), literacy rates, and gender parity in school enrollment highlight educational achievements and disparities. Indicators related to prenatal care, reproductive decision-making, and out-of-pocket health spending reveal ongoing global inequalities in women’s health access. Economic indicators like GDP growth, income distribution, and poverty rates help situate these patterns within broader questions of development and social mobility.
Despite the breadth of this dataset, it is not fully inclusive. Significant portions of the data are missing for many countries and years. High-income countries sometimes have complete, detailed records, while small or low-income countries may be severely underrepresented. Missing data prevented us from using numerous variables that initially appeared promising, limiting the scope of our final analyses. This incomplete coverage introduces silence into the dataset—regions, identities, or experiences that simply do not appear in the statistical record.
Additionally, the dataset only reflects how each national government categorizes gender and reports population statistics. People who identify as women but whose gender is not legally recognized in their country may be excluded. Non-binary and gender-diverse individuals are also absent. In the domain of education, the dataset emphasizes formal educational systems and overlooks informal or community-based learning, which may play a significant role in certain regions.
It is also important to recognize that the World Bank and contributing organizations shape the ontology of this dataset through their own institutional priorities. By emphasizing standardized, measurable indicators aligned with global development goals, they implicitly define progress in terms of quantifiable economic or educational metrics. This framing may marginalize culturally specific or community-defined understandings of gender justice, empowerment, and wellbeing.
Our role as analysts, then, is not only to interpret the available data but also to recognize its limitations; the missing values, the silences, and the institutional frameworks that shape what is counted and what is left out. Understanding these constraints helps us more critically evaluate the patterns we observe and consider the broader context of gender inequality that extends beyond what this dataset can quantify.

Looking at missing values across all variables from 2019–2022, it becomes clear that the indicators that are most incomplete are often the ones that speak most directly to women’s autonomy, health, and lived experience. Many of the variables we were initially most interested in are missing for the vast majority of country–year observations, including:

Reproductive autonomy and decision-making: Variables such as women_3_decisions, informed_repro_health, wanted_fertility_rate, and family_planning_demand are missing in almost all rows. These indicators are supposed to capture whether women can make independent choices about contraception, sexual health, and childbearing. Their absence means that our dataset is largely silent on women’s agency over their own bodies and futures. We can see fertility rates and birth outcomes, but we cannot see whether those outcomes are chosen, coerced, or constrained.
Access to maternal and reproductive health care, and financial risk: Indicators like percent_pregnant_receiving_prenatal_care, prop_spending_more_10_percent_healthcare_oop, and prop_spending_more_25_percent_healthcare_oop also have extremely high missingness. These variables could show which populations are pushed into financial hardship because of health costs, or which pregnant people lack basic prenatal care. Their absence makes it difficult to connect health outcomes to the structural barriers that produce them, and risks portraying maternal health as an individual or cultural issue rather than a question of access and affordability.
Education quality and foundational skills: Several education variables are almost entirely missing, such as gross_intake_ratio_first_grade_F, female_primary_age_oo_school, and female_below_min_reading_proficiency, along with gendered secondary education percentages. These indicators would help us understand not just whether girls are enrolled, but whether they start school on time, stay in school, and achieve minimum reading proficiency. Without them, our view of “education” is flattened into enrollment and completion, and we lose the nuances of who is excluded, who falls behind, and where education systems fail girls most severely.
Distributional economic indicators and poverty: Variables like mean_income_per_cap_bottom_40_percent, prop_ppl_below_50_med_income, and the income shares of the lowest 10% and 20% have substantial gaps. These are precisely the indicators that tie gender to inequality at the bottom of the income distribution. Their absence pushes our analysis toward aggregate measures (like GDP) and away from questions of how gender inequality is experienced by poorer households, rural communities, or marginalized groups within countries.
Structural human capital and health outcomes: Indicators such as HCI (the Human Capital Index) and death_by_infectious_disease_or_maternal_conditions are also heavily missing. These variables could have linked gendered education and health patterns to long-run national capabilities and cause-specific mortality. Instead, their absence keeps our analysis focused on more general outcomes, making it harder to trace how gender inequality is embedded in long-term development trajectories.

At the same time, many of the most “complete” variables in our table—such as gdp, population_total, percent_female_pop, birth_rate, and adolescent_fertility_rate—are high-level demographic or economic indicators with very few missing values. This contrast is revealing: the dataset gives us a fairly consistent view of macro-level trends, but it is much less complete when it comes to the mechanisms of inequality—who has power, who has access, and who is left out of formal systems of care and education.
These patterns of missingness are not random technical flaws; they are themselves a kind of silence. They reflect which indicators countries have the capacity, political will, or institutional priorities to measure, and which experiences remain statistically invisible. By foregrounding these absences alongside the data we do analyze, we can better recognize how the Gender Data Portal both illuminates and obscures different dimensions of gender inequality.

title: Education Investment & School Enrollment
text:
Comparison of education expenditure (as a share of GDP) and primary school enrollment rates in Afghanistan (AFG) and Iceland (ISL) in 2019.


The chart powerfully supports the narrative of a vast development disparity by demonstrating that Iceland significantly outpaces Afghanistan in both educational investment and system reach. Specifically, Iceland’s Education Expenditure (the tall, dark green bar) is nearly three times greater than Afghanistan’s (the short, gold bar), reflecting a superior financial commitment to its education system. Crucially, this higher investment translates directly into systemic success, as Iceland’s Primary School Enrollment Rate is approximately 1.5 times higher than Afghanistan’s, indicating that the Icelandic system has both the resources and the capacity to provide foundational education to a much larger share of its population. This differential in investment and access forms the economic and logistical backdrop that enables Iceland to achieve superior gender equality outcomes, a stark contrast to the challenges faced by Afghanistan.

title: Secondary-Educated Gender Share Low Income Countries
text:
Female share of secondary education enrollment across low–middle income countries in 2018 (top) vs. 2021 (bottom), ordered by infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births). This indicates that access and retention of girls in secondary education greatly improved in the year 2021, following the height of the global pandemic, which called for an emphasis on the importance of education, whether that be virtual or in person(Tamir). Also, by the year 2021 is expected that Sierra Leone will have the highest infant mortality rate, and it will actually become the country with the highest share of secondary completion by females. This demonstrates a huge jump from 2018, where we see that secondary completion rates by females were at 49.5%. This suggests that progress was made in both female health and education fields following the global pandemic, especially due to the high mortality rates that it caused, and the awareness that it shed on preventative health care.
Additionally, while hovering over each bar, we can see the exact infant mortality rate for each country and note that the maximum infant mortality rate for Cape Verde has actually decreased from 58.2% to 54.0% after the pandemic. This could be due to a greater spotlight on education in low-income countries following the outbreak of COVID-19, which would support more online work instead of in-person work that low-income countries often partake in(Akanbi et al. 138–146) We also see a decline in infant mortality due to a greater focus on health, which is a result of more educational opportunities and emphasis. Overall, this visualization illustrated how Covid-19 increased the attention coming from societies on the access to education. As a result there was evident improvement in these two fields. This positive trend followed by the past academic researches that the welfare for women can be significantly improved. (Okui; Pezzulo et al.)Education will make women better understand their reproductive system and more healthcare participation. In the meantime the risk for the pregnant women and the infant will be lower.

title: Adolescent Fertility  by Binned Youth  Labor Force
text:
Adolescent fertility rates (ages 15–24) are displayed for six bins of youth labor force participation. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution of fertility rates within its bin, while the color of each box reflects the median female-to-male literacy ratio for that labor-force-participation range.



While visualization 1 explicitly highlighted how getting education can benefit the health of pregnant women and infants, visualization 2 moved its focus to an even earlier stage of life, shifting its focus to adolescent girls who might not have completed secondary school yet. This visualization helps the audience to understand the economic disadvantage (particularly the participation into the workforce for teenage people) and its relationship to fertility outcomes and literacy levels. These findings supported the wide range of investigations. For researchers such as Azzopardi et al., who emphasize that adolescent wellbeing is shaped by intertwined educational and economic struggles (Azzopardi et al. 1101–1118). Whereas authors such as Singh and Singh argued that the difference when it comes to getting resources due to gender difference can greatly influence a woman’s health conditions (Singh and Singh). From here, the audience can see that visualization 2 demonstrates that labor, education, and reproductive behavior can intersect with each other before a girl turns into an adult.
The visualization illustrates adolescent fertility rates (for females ages 15-24) for six bins of youth labor force participation in order to reveal important connections and relationships between adolescent girls between labor, education, and reproductive behavior. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution of fertility rates within its bin. The color of each box reflects the median female-to-male literacy ratio for that specific labor-force-participation range. In the lowest labor force participation bin, adolescents demonstrate both the lowest average fertility rates and the lowest female-to-male literacy ratios. This suggests that entering and engaging in the workforce may be caused by restricted access to schooling that can thus suppress literacy and childbearing in adolescents. With limited education opportunities, it is linked with lower reproductive knowledge and influence childbearing patterns, consistent with findings from Azzopardi et al. and Akanbi et al., who link limited schooling to higher risks for teenage pregnancy (Akanbi et al. 138–146). Additionally, entering certain forms of work may not require or encourage formal schooling, which can further enforce poor literacy outcomes.
As labor force participation increases, average fertility rates increase slightly, but fertility outcomes vary the most, particularly in the 33.5–40.4 participation bin. This displays the greatest variability and can indicate that adolescents who enter the workforce at higher rates might be doing so at ages that experience close to or peak fertility years. The visualization illustrates that the highest labor force participation groups also happen to contain some of the highest fertility values. This goes against the idea that greater economic stability leads to delayed fertility amongst adolescent females. Instead, the visualization suggests that high adolescent labor participation may lead to early work and parenthood (Zeng et al.; Singh and Singh).
Overall the second visualization showcased the importance of understanding the relationship between adolescent labor behaviors in a broader social and economic contexts. That adolescent groups working is not only an economical indicator, but it’s highly related to literacy rates, access to education and giving birth to the next generation. This chart emphasized the core of our project, that education is a crucial indicator of the health status of women. The impact can be long standing even before adulthood.

title: Case Study
text:
A Case Study into Afghanistan and Iceland: Investment and Equity
While our analysis helps us understand the broad global relationship between GDP, health expenditure, and neonatal mortality, these correlations will become clearer with a comparison between two countries. We chose to do a case study of Afghanistan and Iceland to show how different countries can have completely different outcomes on healthcare and gender equality depending on their national investment.



Comparison of education expenditure (as a share of GDP) and primary school enrollment rates in Afghanistan (AFG) and Iceland (ISL) in 2019.


The comparison between Afghanistan and Iceland reveals a direct correlation between national investment in education and the achievement of gender equity within the system. By normalizing all metrics to a 0-100 scale, the data clearly shows that Iceland’s Normalized Expenditure is leveraged into near-perfect gender parity, as evidenced by both its Primary Female Share Percentage and Lower Secondary Female Percentage hovering at the ideal mark of approximately 50% female enrollment.
Conversely, Afghanistan’s significantly lower normalized expenditure results in substantial gender inequity across its education system. The Afghan data shows the female share dropping from a low of 39% at the primary level to approximately 37% at the lower secondary level. This steep decline implies that not only is the total system under-resourced, but that systemic barriers disproportionately increase as girls attempt to advance to higher levels of education, strongly supporting the narrative that national investment is a prerequisite for achieving and sustaining equitable societal outcomes.



Comparison of birth and mortality-related health metrics in Afghanistan and Iceland.

This educational disparity has severe health implications: lower levels of female education correlate strongly with higher rates of adolescent fertility and death by infectious disease or maternal conditions. The lack of schooling in Afghanistan is not only an equity issue but also a profound public health crisis, limiting women’s knowledge of basic sanitation, reproductive health, and when to seek medical care, thereby perpetuating a cycle of low educational attainment and high mortality rates that Iceland’s system has successfully broken.
The selection of Iceland and Afghanistan for this comparative analysis is driven by their representation of two geopolitical and developmental extremes on the spectrum of gender equality and human development. Iceland consistently ranks at the top of global indices for gender equality, notably achieving remarkable parity in education, economic participation, and political empowerment. Conversely, Afghanistan, particularly during the period analyzed, has been widely documented as facing severe, systemic challenges regarding women’s rights and access to essential services, including education. The deliberate contrast between Iceland’s model of high, equitable investment and Afghanistan’s documented limitations, especially concerning female secondary school access, creates a clear case study. This divergence maximizes the potential for observing and quantifying the effects of social investment (or lack thereof) on fundamental indicators like mortality rates, educational attainment, and overall public health outcomes.

title: Narrative
text:
Education and healthcare are two powerful factors shaping the life qualities for women around the globe, but the relationship between them varies significantly by country based on their level of development. During times when countries are trying to solve problems with education inequality, gaps in healthcare resources, and problematic gender stereotypes, it’s crucial to look at the question of how the level of education women receive can influence their health outcomes. From a macro perspective, global indicators had evident contrasts. We see this in the Average Birth Rate Per Country map below, as it shows major regional disparities in fertility and health expenditure. These inequalities led to the central question of our project, which is “How does women’s education shape reproductive, maternal, and overall health outcomes across countries?”.
To investigate this question, we as a team conducted research on the World Bank’s gender data portal to see the long-term trend of gender, health, and socioeconomic development. These datasets incorporated information and statistics from the United Nations and also the national statistical offices, as well as international health and labor organizations. This dataset is highly relevant to our research because it provides standardized and internationally comparable statistical data from 2000-2022. The datasets contained variables such as school enrollment, adolescent fertility, maternal healthcare access, gender parity indexes, and health expenditures. After thorough data cleaning and processing, our team applied Tableau and R software to create visualizations like scatterplots linking health expenditure, adolescent fertility, and birth rate. These data visualizations demonstrate that there is a significant positive correlation between a woman’s level of education and their healthcare-related issues. The chosen dataset provided the foundation to our central thesis, that the investment in women’s education not only can improve their healthcare outcomes, but also promotes a broader level of socioeconomic welfare support.

title: Narrative
section: What is the relationship between women’s participation in education and birth rates in major developing countries?
text:
What is the relationship between women’s participation in education and birth rates in major developing countries?


 

Female share of secondary education enrollment across low–middle income countries in 2018 (top) vs. 2021 (bottom), ordered by infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births). Each bar displays the proportion of secondary students who are female versus male. The dashed line marks the 45% female-share threshold to highlight countries falling below this benchmark.



Female share of secondary education enrollment across low–middle income countries in 2018 (top) vs. 2021 (bottom), ordered by infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births). Each bar displays the proportion of secondary students who are female versus male. The dashed line marks the 45% female-share threshold to highlight countries falling below this benchmark.


To explore the relationship between female participation in secondary education and birth rates in developing countries, this visualization compares female shares of secondary education completion rates across low to middle-income countries in the years 2018 (top) and 2021 (bottom), ordered by infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births), where the left of the visualization indicates low infant mortality rates and the right side indicates high reports of infant mortality. Each bar reflects the proportion of secondary students who are female (green) versus male (yellow). The dashed line marks the 45% female-share threshold. Our group selected the years 2018 and 2021 to demonstrate how the COVID-19 pandemic affected girls’ secondary education and infant mortality outcomes.
In 2018, it is important to note that the majority of countries just barely meet the 45% female share benchmark, but by 2021, nearly all in the dataset will exceed this standard. This indicates that access and retention of girls in secondary education greatly improved in the year 2021, following the height of the global pandemic, which called for an emphasis on the importance of education, whether that be virtual or in person (Tamir). Also, it is expected that Sierra Leone will have the highest infant mortality rate, and it will actually become the country with the highest share of secondary completion by females in 2021. This demonstrates a huge jump from 2018, where we see that secondary completion rates by females were at 49.5%. This suggests that progress was made in both female health and education fields following the global pandemic, especially due to the high mortality rates that it caused and the awareness that it shed on preventative health care.
Additionally, while hovering over each bar, we can see the exact infant mortality rate for each country and note that the maximum infant mortality rate for Cape Verde has actually decreased from 58.2% to 54.0% after the pandemic. This could be due to a greater spotlight on education in low-income countries following the outbreak of COVID-19, which would support more online work instead of in-person work that low-income countries often partake in (Akanbi et al. 138–146) We also see a decline in infant mortality due to a greater focus on health, which is a result of more educational opportunities and emphasis.
Overall, this visualization illustrated how the Covid-19 pandemic heightened societal focus on the critical importance of education access, and this increased attention likely contributed to the evident improvement observed in both female secondary enrollment and infant mortality outcomes by 2021. This positive trend aligns with established academic research (Okui; Pezzulo et al.) demonstrating that investments in women’s education significantly improve their welfare. Education empowers women with a better understanding of their reproductive health and fosters increased participation in healthcare, ultimately leading to lower risks for both pregnant women and infants.
Before analyzing the next visualization, it is crucial to recognize how women’s early educational experiences form the foundation for their future education and health outcomes. While our first visualization focused on the link between birth rates and secondary education, examining primary school completion allows us to better understand where gender inequality originates. These early disparities are cumulative, not only hindering women’s ability to access higher education but also shaping the long-term fertility patterns and health risks discussed in our literature review.



Line chart comparing gender gaps in primary school completion from 2018–2022 for the three highest-GDP and three lowest-GDP countries. High-GDP countries cluster near zero, showing minimal gender differences and little variation over time. Low-GDP countries show much larger positive and negative gender gaps, with substantial year-to-year fluctuation, indicating both greater inequality and less stability in completion rates.


This visualization deepens our investigation by demonstrating the gender gaps in primary school completion rates between countries with high and low GDP for the years 2018–2022. Though classified by economic level, this analysis remains central to our research question, as early age education patterns significantly influence later fertility behaviors. The data shows more evident volatility and pronounced gender gaps in primary school completion rates for both men and women in low-GDP countries. Contrastingly, the completion rate in high-GDP countries is relatively stable and exhibits minimal gender disparity. This pattern of instability is crucial, as primary education serves as the foundation for all subsequent educational opportunities. Regions where girls fall behind early are precisely where scholars like Azzopardi and Pezzulo identify patterns of higher adolescent fertility and birth rates (Azzopardi et al. 1108; Pezzulo et al. e806–07). Conversely, the stability observed in higher-GDP countries is reflected in lower birth rates, a social environment where women have better access to healthcare, and greater reproductive autonomy. Thus, this visualization directly highlights the fact that early education inequalities create the groundwork for major reproductive inequality in developing nations.
Moreover, this visualization demonstrated that instability in primary school education has direct repercussions for broader maternal and infant health outcomes. Countries with large gender gaps in primary completion, primarily those in the low-GDP range, face a heightened risk of insufficient healthcare problems, including higher teenage pregnancy rates, limited access to essential care, and elevated infant mortality. Women with limited early education encounter a greater systemic obstacle in accessing healthcare support, particularly in rural and economically struggling areas (Singh). This finding is reinforced by Okui’s work, which demonstrated that even a minimal difference in parental education levels can impact the risk of preterm birth (Okui). Furthermore, Ran’s research highlights that combining educational opportunities with informational tools, such as the internet, can actively reduce the maternal mortality rate (Ran, 1275-77). Collectively, these research studies reinforce the critical finding that the instability of women’s early education, or systematic gender inequalities, precipitates higher birth rates and the deterioration of healthcare, while stable and equitable access to education establishes the necessary foundation for positive maternal and infant health outcomes.

title: Narrative
section: How do female adolescent reproductive outcomes vary across literacy levels and labor force participation?
text:
How do female adolescent reproductive outcomes vary across literacy levels and labor force participation?


 

Adolescent fertility rates (ages 15–24) are displayed for six bins of youth labor force participation. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution of fertility rates within its bin, while the color of each box reflects the median female-to-male literacy ratio for that labor-force-participation range.



Building on the previous two visualizations that focused on early educational inequalities, our third visualization shifts perspective to adolescence. This stage is critical because the educational gaps women face in their early years have a long-term, cumulative impact that significantly shapes their reproductive outcomes. In contrast to the second visualization, which examined foundational education patterns, this one primarily depicts the link between economic disadvantage (specifically, youth labor force participation) and its relationship to fertility outcomes and literacy levels. These findings align with a broad range of scholarly investigations. Researchers like Azzopardi et al. emphasize that adolescent well-being is shaped by intertwined educational and economic struggles (Azzopardi et al. 1101–1118), while authors such as Singh argue that gender differences in resource access profoundly influence a woman’s health conditions (Singh). Ultimately, this visualization demonstrates how labor, education, and reproductive behavior intersect and influence female adolescents before they transition into adulthood.
The visualization illustrates adolescent fertility rates (for females ages 15–24) across six distinct bins of youth labor force participation, revealing important connections between labor, education, and reproductive behavior in adolescent females. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution of fertility rates within its respective bin, and the color of each box reflects the median female-to-male literacy ratio for that specific labor-force-participation range.
In the lowest labor force participation bin, adolescents demonstrate both the lowest average fertility rates and the lowest female-to-male literacy ratios. This finding suggests a complex relationship where marginalization and restricted access to schooling may limit both economic activity and childbearing. While limited education is linked to lower reproductive knowledge and influences childbearing patterns, a finding consistent with Azzopardi et al. and Akanbi et al., who link limited schooling to higher risks for teenage pregnancy (Akanbi et al. 138–146), the lowest participation may represent a group facing systemic barriers that suppress all forms of measured activity. Furthermore, the forms of work available to this group often do not require or encourage formal schooling, which perpetuates poor literacy outcomes and reinforces the cycle of marginalization.
As labor force participation increases, the average fertility rate rises slightly, but fertility outcomes exhibit the greatest variability, particularly in the 33.5–40.4 participation bin. This high variance may indicate that adolescents entering the workforce at higher rates are often doing so during their peak fertility years. Crucially, the visualization illustrates that the highest labor force participation groups also contain some of the highest fertility values. This finding runs counter to the established trend in developed economies, where economic stability is typically associated with delayed fertility. Instead, the data suggests that in these contexts, high adolescent labor participation may be driven by poverty and the necessity of early work, which in turn facilitates or precedes early parenthood (Zeng et al.; Singh).
Overall, the third visualization showcases the vital importance of understanding adolescent labor behaviors within a broader social and economic context. For young women, participation in the workforce is not solely an economic indicator; it is highly intertwined with literacy rates, access to education, and reproductive behavior. This chart powerfully reinforces the main hypothesis of our project: education is a crucial indicator of the health status of women, and its impact is long-standing, shaping outcomes well before they reach full adulthood.

title: Narrative
section: Why do countries with similar or different GDP levels exhibit dissimilar Neonatal mortality rates, and how might health expenditure and variations in women’s education explain these differences?
text:
Why do countries with similar or different GDP levels exhibit dissimilar Neonatal mortality rates, and how might health expenditure and variations in women’s education explain these differences?


 

Each point represents a country in a given year, where the x-axis reflects economic size (log GDP), the y-axis reflects neonatal mortality, and the color indicates health expenditure per capita.



Exploring visualizations that observe on the macro level with specific comparisons with micro level healthcare spending was an aspect we desired to analyze as a potential way to showcase how economic forces can influence health outcomes. This visualization in particular applies a log scale to GDP to reduce the extreme spread in values and allow patterns to be more easily interpreted. The results show that health expenditure per capita is far more strongly associated with neonatal mortality than GDP itself. The color gradient makes this clear: countries with higher health spending consistently exhibit lower neonatal mortality rates, regardless of their GDP level.
Interestingly, across the middle of the GDP distribution, we observe a concentration of countries largely lower- to middle-income economies with notably higher neonatal mortality rates. In contrast, both the lowest-GDP and highest-GDP countries show similar ranges of neonatal mortality outcomes, suggesting that GDP alone is not a reliable predictor of neonatal survival. This reinforces the idea that investment in health systems, rather than economic size, is what directly improves neonatal outcomes. Moreover, this also reinforces the idea that “higher-educated mothers have better access to healthcare services and resources, including quality antenatal care and skilled birth attendants, which can lead to timely interventions and improved neonatal outcomes”, as evidenced by investment in healthcare systems (Tamir 6). When women are more highly educated and have quality access to healthcare through increased health expenditure, neonatal mortality rates decrease, and overall reproductive and early childhood health increases.
The visualization, therefore, highlights that increased health expenditure has a more immediate and measurable impact on reducing neonatal mortality than broad economic indicators. It is significant to showcase the wide range of investment in healthcare that clearly displays that increased attention and accessibility to healthcare will enable overall health outcomes to increase. Policies that improve women’s access to healthcare, prenatal services, and skilled birth assistance can directly reduce neonatal mortality, even in countries with modest GDP levels.
Researcher Tadesse Tarik Tamir at the University of Gondar in Ethiopia has conducted extensive research on the topic of neonatal mortality and the intersectional factors associated with higher rates of neonatal mortality, including low or no maternal education and neonates that are born in countries with low literacy rates (Tamir 7). Coming from a country that is relatively middle-income, experiencing high neonatal mortality rates, and very low health expenditure per capita according to the visualization, Tamir has first-hand experience and analysis on how women’s education can truly impact the health outcomes that come with it. In this case, because health expenditure is directly linked to how accessible a healthcare service is, this visualization is key to looking at how it indirectly reflects mechanisms through which women’s education can improve maternal and infant/neonatal health.
Therefore, this visualization highlighted that, compared to macroeconomic indicators, increasing the expenditure on health is more directly related to lowering the infant mortality rates. It’s crucial to display a wide range of investment in health-related medical fields, which clearly shows that the increase of attention and making healthcare more accessible can push for the overall improvement of health outcomes. Even in countries with lower GDP, the advancement of healthcare through policy making in prenatal services, skilled birth assistance can reduce the mortality rate. Researcher Tadesse Tarik Tamir, for example, showed that there’s a strong positive correlation between the infant’s mortality rates to the low level of maternal education and low national literacy rates (Tamir 7). His work depicted to the public that the infant health outcome can’t be separated from women’s education.

title: About
text:
Our Project
We are a team of UCLA students investigating how women’s education shapes health outcomes across countries at varying stages of development. Our research explores how education serves as a critical determinant of women’s health by influencing fertility behavior, access to healthcare, and overall knowledge about reproductive and maternal health, particularly focusing on pre-post COVID influences. We argue that higher levels of education among women correlate with lower fertility rates, as education often delays marriage and childbearing while increasing awareness and use of family planning methods. Moreover, education enhances women’s ability to navigate healthcare systems such as improving access to prenatal and postnatal care, child immunization, and preventive services.
Beyond access, education empowers women with the knowledge to make informed health decisions, challenge harmful cultural norms, and advocate for their own well-being. By comparing data across countries at different stages of economic and social development, our project seeks to highlight how investments in women’s education not only improve individual health outcomes but also generate broader societal benefits, including reduced maternal mortality, healthier families, and more sustainable population growth. We believe this will allow us to produce a meaningful and inclusive project that will enable individuals around the world to understand our research question.

Sources
The primary source for our data is the Gender Data Portal, created and funded by the World Bank Group. The portal is maintained by the World Bank’s Gender Group and the Development Economics Data Group, who update the dataset four times per year. Its development and continued improvement are also supported by several multi-donor trust funds, including the Umbrella Facility for Gender Equality, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and other long-term contributors.
Data featured in the Gender Data Portal is collected by national governments and major international organizations responsible for producing official, gender-disaggregated statistics. These contributors include national statistical offices, ministries of labor, health, education, and population, as well as international bodies such as UNDP, UNICEF, UN Women, UNESCO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). These organizations gather standardized data from member countries, which the World Bank compiles and organizes within the Gender Data Portal to make global comparisons accessible and reliable.
We wanted to acknowledge the potential bias or silence that could be created and produced due to the nature of the World Bank and other International Non-Governmental Organizations that have been known to insert their own politics into the data that they present. This could inherently shape the ontology of the data and skew the interpretation of the argument that we are trying to convey. Although this can be the case, we believe the standardized data that has been utilized in the creation of this project by the World Bank offers the most accurate and wide range of data that encompasses and acknowledges everything that needs to be included to the best of our ability.


Processing
Because our data came directly from the Gender Data Portal, we retrieved each indicator individually through the API using its specific variable code. Each variable was provided in a long format indexed by economy (country code) with a separate column for every year. To prepare the dataset for analysis, we performed extensive preprocessing in Python using libraries such as pandas and numpy. This included reshaping each variable into a consistent structure where year existed as a single column, allowing us to merge the indicators into one larger multi-variable dataset.
After assembling the cleaned dataset, we exported a raw CSV containing 32 variables. To maintain transparency and avoid introducing misleading patterns, we chose not to use imputations for any key variables. Instead, we restricted our analysis to the subset of countries and years where data were actually available. For example, variables such as primary and lower-secondary education completion rates for females had substantial missingness—nearly 30%, which meant that using the full dataset would have required artificially filling gaps or relying on unreliable estimates. Rather than compromise the integrity of our findings, we limited certain analyses to countries with complete data for the time periods we were comparing (e.g., pre- and post-COVID).
This subsetting inevitably constrained the number of countries represented in portions of our analysis, but it allowed us to prioritize ethical data practices and maintain analytical accuracy. As discussed in our data critique, missing data is not random; the absence of indicators in certain countries or years may reflect structural, political, or institutional factors. By choosing not to impute missing values and instead analyze only the available records, we acknowledge these silences and avoid unintentionally distorting patterns in gender inequality.
For our visualizations, we used Tableau and R to highlight patterns in the data. Tableau powered interactive dashboards that were easy for teammates with less coding experience to build and explore, while R supported more technical, analysis-heavy charts. Some of our team members also leveraged the Plotly library in R to add interactivity to custom graphics. In addition, we used Timeline.js to create an interactive chronology of global birth rates that paired narrative context with visuals.


Presentation
Our site was developed in RStudio using Quarto, hosted on Netlify, and version-controlled with GitHub. The website has a white and mint color palette and texts are in black color to enhance the readability of the website using contrast. Every picture and data visualizations have alt text and descriptive headers to assist readers in their understanding. All headers follows a HTML structure which improves the accessibility of our website and provides directions for users when navigating.
To visualize our research outcomes, our website integrats several data visualizations of different variables in our data. The purpose of this was to understand how the level of education for women can impact the right of getting healthcare in different countries. Based on the data collected from the World Bank’s Gender Data Portal, our visualizations highlighted the intersectionality between education, gender equality, birth rate and the holistic social welfare of different societies. Through this work, our goal is to turn statistical data into a human centered narration that explores how education shapes women’s health and futures beyond the classroom.

title: About
text:
Generative AI Disclaimer
Generative AI was used as a support tool to reword and tighten sections of the written narrative for clarity, flow, and accessibility, while all core ideas, arguments, and interpretations were developed by our group. It was also used to help debug and refine code related to our visualizations and website creation (e.g., adjusting Quarto/HTML structure, iframe embeds, and alt text for accessibility), but all data selection, analytical decisions, and visualization designs were determined independently by us.

title: GDP vs. Neonatal Mortality Rates
text:
Each point represents a country in a given year, where the x-axis reflects economic size (log GDP), the y-axis reflects neonatal mortality, and the color indicates health expenditure per capita.



This visualization explores and compares a country’s neonatal mortality rates versus the economic size (GDP) and the health expenditure that each country endows. This visualization in particular applies a log scale to GDP to reduce the extreme spread in values and allow patterns to be more easily interpreted. The results show that health expenditure per capita is far more strongly associated with neonatal mortality than GDP itself. The color gradient makes this clear: countries with higher health spending consistently exhibit lower neonatal mortality rates, regardless of their GDP level. Interestingly, across the middle of the GDP distribution, we observe a concentration of countries—largely lower- to middle-income economies—with notably higher neonatal mortality rates. In contrast, both the lowest-GDP and highest-GDP countries show similar ranges of neonatal mortality outcomes, suggesting that GDP alone is not a reliable predictor of neonatal survival. This reinforces the idea that investment in health systems, rather than economic size, is what directly improves neonatal outcomes. Moreover, this also reinforces the idea that “higher-educated mothers have better access to healthcare services and resources, including quality antenatal care and skilled birth attendants, which can lead to timely interventions and improved neonatal outcomes” that are showcased through investment in healthcare systems. When women are more highly educated and have quality access to healthcare through increased health expenditure, neonatal mortality rates decrease, and overall reproductive and early childhood health increases. The visualization therefore, highlights that increased health expenditure has a more immediate and measurable impact on reducing neonatal mortality than broad economic indicators. Policies that improve women’s access to healthcare, prenatal services, and skilled birth assistance can directly reduce neonatal mortality, even in countries with modest GDP levels.

title: Gender Gap Primary School Completion  Before, During, &After Pandemic
text:
How does the gender gap in primary school completion differ between countries of high and low economic development, and what can this reveal about global patterns of gender inequality in education?
There are much larger gender disparities in the countries with the lowest 3 GDPs than the countries with the highest 3 GDPS. Some countries experience female disadvantages, while others experience female advantages. The variability in these countries is high, suggesting that gender inequality in these countries is less stable and possibly more sensitive to year-by-year changes like social or economic shifts. In contrast, high GDP countries cluster near zero, indicating that boys and girls complete primary school at nearly equal rates. Not only that, but they have much smaller variability, indicating that access to education is relatively equal between genders through global changes (for example, the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic). Because we can see that some countries in the low-GDP group see higher rates of girls’ education and others see higher rates of boys’, this visualization highlights that gender equality is shaped not only by the economy but also by cultural and political reforms in each country.
